title: How to give design feedback without restarting the project
metaTitle: Design feedback that does not restart
excerpt: Give feedback against the goal: clearer, more serious, or easier to scan. Redesigning in the margin restarts the work unless the goal itself was wrong.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The label is the right target for feedback: the goal, before anyone redraws the screen.
caption: React to the goal written on the page. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is useful design feedback?
faqs.answer: Useful feedback names the goal and what is failing it. Clearer, more serious, or easier to scan are usable reactions. Point at the part of the screen that causes the problem, and say what a stranger should understand or do. Leave the new layout to the person designing, unless the goal itself was wrong.

faqs.question: What kind of feedback restarts the work?
faqs.answer: A new direction in the margin restarts the work: a different structure, a different audience, or a sketch of a new page attached to a review of the current one. So does a pile of personal taste with no goal, delivered after the direction was approved. Park those notes. They are a new brief, or they are noise.

faqs.question: How many people should send feedback?
faqs.answer: One approver should send the decision. Others can comment earlier, in the same channel, and the approver resolves conflicts before the note goes to the studio. Five contradictory markups are five restarts. A single note with the disagreements already settled is a review.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
How to give design feedback that keeps the project moving: react to the goal. Say whether the work is clearer, more serious, or easier to scan. Redesign in the margin only when the goal itself was wrong.

Feedback is a decision about the work in front of you, measured against something you already agreed. A second design, delivered as comments, throws the round away.

## Name the goal first

Every review needs a sentence you can fail. “The homepage helps a stranger see what this is and how to talk to us.” “The product page explains the object, then lets someone buy it.” “The empty state tells a new user what to do next.” If the goal is missing, feedback becomes taste, and taste does not converge.

Write the goal at the top of the note, even if you think everyone remembers it. Then react. The goal is the sheet the work is pinned to. A user-flow labeled with user goals is the same idea on paper: the goals are visible, so the drawing can be judged.

Nielsen Norman Group’s [research on how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), from 2011, is a useful goal for anything public. The first ten seconds are when a visitor is most likely to leave, and a clear value proposition is what earns more of their time. “Clearer,” on a homepage, often means that proposition is still late, vague, or competing with a brand line that does not say what the company does. You can give that note without drawing a new hero. Say what the stranger still cannot answer.

If you cannot name the goal, do not mark up the file yet. Ask for the goal, or propose one, and agree it before the pixels move again. Markup without a goal feels productive and sends the work sideways.

## Three reactions that help

Most useful notes are one of three, pointed at a specific part of the screen.

Clearer. Something a stranger must understand is still muddy. The headline, the price, the next step, the error. Say what you thought it meant, and what you needed it to mean. “I read this as a marketplace. We are one brand’s shop.” That is a brief the designer can use. “Pop more” is not.

More serious. The tone is too playful, too loud, or too casual for the promise. Point at the element that causes it: a illustration style, a joke in the button, a color that fights the photography. Serious does not mean gray. It means the voice matches the offer you already chose. If the verbal identity says you will not sound breathless, a breathless subhead is a miss against that rule.

Easier to scan. The hierarchy is flat, or the page asks for reading before it offers a decision. Name what should be seen first, second, and third. A dashboard should show what changed, what needs a decision, and what can wait. A product grid should let the eye compare objects, which is a crop and a price more than a paragraph. You are describing order, not designing the replacement.

One note can contain all three. Keep each to a few lines. A review that is a letter will be skimmed, and the important line will be the one that happened to sound sharpest, not the one that mattered.

## What restarts the work

These patterns throw away the round. Use them only when you mean to.

A sketch of a different page in the margin. You have become the designer, without the constraints, and the studio must now either build your sketch or spend the review arguing with it. If the sketch is the point, call it a new direction and accept the date. If it is a suggestion, say “the goal is failing in this way” and let them solve it.

A new audience halfway through. “Also make it work for investors and for hiring” is a different site. Park it. The current goal was a buyer. Adding two jobs to the first screen is how the page becomes a hallway.

Taste with no failure attached. “I don’t like green.” “Can we try a serif?” “My partner prefers the other concept.” Preferences are allowed at the moment you pick a direction. After the direction is accepted, a preference needs a goal. If the serif makes the heritage brand more serious, say that. If it is only familiarity, it can wait for a later experiment.

Late feedback from someone who missed the approval. Their note may be good. It is still late. The approver decides whether it is a change, with a date attached, or a note for the next slice. Silent inclusion is how the project restarts without anyone choosing to restart it.

A pile of small visual edits that add up to a new layout. Moving every block, restating every heading, and swapping every image in one round is a new design. Call it that. Or cut the list to the edits that serve the goal, and hold the rest.

## How to write the note

One approver sends one note. Collect other comments first if you need to, resolve the contradictions, and send the result. Five people writing in the file will not average out into a clear page. They will average out into a committee page, which is the look you were trying to leave.

Use this shape.

- Goal, in one sentence.
- What is working, so it does not get “fixed.”
- What is failing the goal, each item named and located.
- What you are not asking to reopen.

“What is working” is not politeness. It is scope protection. If the type is right, say so, or the next round will restyle it while fixing a headline. If the photography crop is right, say so, or a well-meant tweak will mix the frames.

Locate the comment. “The paragraph under the price,” not “the copy.” “The second size in the list,” not “variants.” A located note can be done. A global mood cannot.

Ask for a change in outcome, then stop. “A first-time visitor should know this is a single product studio and see the intro call without scrolling on a phone.” That is enough. You do not need to specify the font size, the exact line break, and a new illustration in the same breath. Specify those only when they are the brand system and the system was violated.

Time-box your own review. If you cannot respond in the window you agreed, say so before the window closes, and say what the delay does to the date. Silence followed by a redesign is the most expensive kind of feedback.

## When the goal was wrong

Sometimes the work hits the goal and the goal is the problem. The page is clear, and you realize you are describing the wrong offer. The interface is easy to scan, and you realize the workflow is not the one customers have.

Say that plainly. “The goal was wrong. We are not a marketplace. Stop this direction.” That note is allowed to restart the work, because you are choosing the restart with your eyes open. It should come with the new goal in a sentence, and with an acceptance that the date moves.

Do this as soon as you know. A wrong goal gets more expensive every round you decorate it. A studio that will not hear “the goal was wrong” is stuck. A founder who whispers it as a series of visual complaints will get a restless page and a confused team. Hanabi’s process is meant to change when the offer changes. The change has to be named.

Then hold the new goal still long enough to judge the next round against it. A project that gets a new goal every review is not iterating. It is declining to decide.

If you want a room where this kind of note is the whole agenda, the method is a critique. The short version for a small team is [how to run a design critique](/blog/design-critique-for-small-teams).

When you want a partner who will take this kind of feedback and keep the date honest, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the goal you think the work is for. The call can test whether it is the right one before a project starts.
